criteria.descriptor: Accurately describes MCP's `initialize`/version negotiation, correctly separates breaking from backward-compatible schema changes, correctly names token passthrough plus confused deputy and the audience-binding fix (resource server + RFC 8707 + downstream token exchange), and correctly characterizes tool poisoning/rug-pull and Streamable HTTP transport hardening. No fabricated mechanisms or misused terms.

Addresses all four required parts — version negotiation, safe schema evolution including the required-parameter case, the authorization redesign, and at least two additional protocol-level attacks with mitigations — with concrete mechanisms rather than leaving any part unaddressed.

Explains why each flaw is dangerous (silent version mismatch, immediate breakage of independent clients, audience bypass and blast radius, post-approval mutation) and why each proposed fix resolves it, explicitly weighing backward compatibility for existing clients against the need to change.
Reads as a design review with a clear critique-versus-redesign separation, uses precise protocol vocabulary correctly, and gives actionable, specific recommendations rather than vague advice.

expected_answer_points: Requires the MCP `initialize` handshake exchanging `protocolVersion` (date-based) and `capabilities`, gating tool calls and optional features behind the negotiated version/capabilities, and explains that no version field causes silent shape/capability mismatch and blocks safe future evolution.
Correctly classifies adding a required parameter as a breaking change and prescribes additive-only evolution: new fields optional with defaults, never remove or retype a field in place.
Handles required-input changes safely by introducing a new or versioned tool that runs in parallel, with deprecation/sunset signaling and client migration before retiring the old one.
Names 'token passthrough' as the anti-pattern and identifies the confused-deputy attack (audience/`aud` bypass, expanded blast radius) it enables.

Prescribes the correct auth model: MCP server as OAuth 2.1 resource server with audience-restricted, least-privilege tokens minted for it (Resource Indicators / RFC 8707), full token validation, separately-scoped downstream credential via token exchange rather than replaying the inbound token, plus explicit consent.

Identifies tool poisoning / rug pull (untrusted descriptions and unpinned schemas mutating post-approval) with mitigations such as pinning/hashing definitions, diff-and-re-consent, and treating descriptions as untrusted.
Identifies transport/session hardening for Streamable HTTP (TLS, Origin validation against DNS-rebinding, unpredictable user-bound session IDs, no tokens in URLs).
common_pitfalls: Treating the new required parameter as safe to 'just add and tell clients to update', ignoring that dozens of independent clients validate and break the instant the schema redeploys.

Accepting token passthrough because 'it is the user's own token so it is authorized', missing that audience/scope binding is the whole point, or 'fixing' it only with TLS/encryption instead of audience-restricted tokens and downstream token exchange.
Confusing product/API SemVer with protocol version negotiation and never mentioning the MCP `initialize` handshake or capability negotiation.
Listing generic web vulnerabilities (SQL injection, XSS, rate limiting) instead of protocol-level agent threats such as tool poisoning, rug pull, confused deputy, and session hijacking.
Conflating authentication with authorization — validating that a token is well-signed but not that it was issued for this server with the right scopes and audience.
Assuming the newest protocol version can simply be forced on every client, breaking older clients, rather than negotiating down to a mutually supported version.
reference_answer:
(1) Version negotiation. MCP runs on JSON-RPC 2.0 and mandates an `initialize` handshake before any tool traffic: the client sends the `protocolVersion` it supports (MCP uses date-based version strings such as "2025-06-18") plus its `capabilities`, and the server replies with the version it will actually speak and its own capabilities. If the server does not support the client's version it returns the latest it does support, and the client decides whether to proceed or disconnect. Skipping this handshake means the two ends can silently disagree about message shapes, capability sets, and security expectations; there is then no safe way to introduce any future protocol change, and optional features (streaming, elicitation) get assumed rather than negotiated. Redesign: require `initialize` first, reject `tools/call` before a successful handshake, negotiate a mutually supported version, and gate optional behaviors behind the negotiated `capabilities`.

(2) Schema evolution. Adding a new *required* parameter is a breaking change: existing clients do not send it, so their calls fail validation the moment you redeploy. The rule is additive/backward-compatible evolution — new fields must be optional with a safe default, and you never remove or retype a field in place. To actually require new input, introduce a *new* tool (or a versioned tool name/endpoint) that runs in parallel with the old one, mark the old tool deprecated with sunset signaling, migrate clients, and retire the old tool only after the sunset window. Version/capability negotiation lets you expose the new tool only to clients that understand it. Editing schemas in place is an unannounced breaking change and also a rug-pull vector (below).

(3) Token handling. Forwarding the end-user's web-app token to the billing API is the 'token passthrough' anti-pattern, explicitly forbidden by MCP's authorization guidance. That token's audience is the web app, not the MCP server or the billing API, so `aud`/audience validation is bypassed; with the MCP server acting as intermediary this is a classic *confused deputy* — the server uses a trusted position or a token never scoped for the downstream call to do things the caller could not authorize directly, expanding blast radius and destroying auditability and least privilege. Correct model: treat the MCP server as an OAuth 2.1 *resource server* with its own identifier; require tokens minted specifically for it (audience-restricted via Resource Indicators / RFC 8707) with least-privilege scopes; validate signature, issuer, audience, expiry and scope on every request; and for the billing call have the server obtain its own separately-scoped credential (token exchange / on-behalf-of, or a service credential) instead of replaying the inbound token. Per-client user consent must gate authorization to avoid static-client confused-deputy consent bypass.

(4) Further attacks. (a) Tool poisoning / rug pull: because descriptions and schemas are fetched fresh and trusted as-is, hidden instructions can be embedded in a tool description (prompt injection at the client's model) or a tool's behavior/schema can change *after* it was approved (rug pull). Mitigate by pinning and hashing approved tool definitions, diffing changes and re-prompting for consent when they change, and treating descriptions as untrusted data, not instructions. (b) Session/transport weaknesses on Streamable HTTP: mitigate with mandatory TLS, `Origin` header validation to block DNS-rebinding/cross-origin abuse, cryptographically random session IDs bound to the authenticated user, and never putting tokens in URLs.
